utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-67-PT, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. May I have the appearances? Prosecution first.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Hildegard Uertz-Retzlaff for the Prosecution with our case manager Ana Katalinic. And my name is Dan Saxon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Saxon. I see that stand-by counsel, Mr. Hooper and Mr. O'Shea as co-stand-by counsel are present. The Chamber also establishes that Mr. Seselj, who is self-represented, is not present. And the first thing the Chamber would like to do is to inquire into the absence and the reasons for it. I see that Mr. Vincent -- you're acting Deputy Registrar of this Tribunal. You're here, I take it, in anticipation of questions by this Chamber on what happened this morning, since Mr. Seselj seems not to appear. Could you tell us what happened this morning when, I take it, as usual, Mr. Seselj was invited to be ready for transportation to the Tribunal and to appear at this Status Conference?

utterances.speaker: MR. VINCENT
utterances.text: Your Honours, yes, I can confirm he was seen by the commander of the Detention Unit and intimated that he felt too weak to attend the hearing this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And did he express what the reason was for feeling too weak?

utterances.speaker: MR. VINCENT
utterances.text: Well, he said that his voice was not as strong as he would like and he was not keen on the transportation arrangements. He felt that he wouldn't be able to stand up to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did he ask for any additional facilities, for example, wheelchair or --

utterances.speaker: MR. VINCENT
utterances.text: He's asked for nothing, Your Honours, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Can you explain what were the reasons for that weak state?

utterances.speaker: MR. VINCENT
utterances.text: The reasons for the weak state are that Mr. Seselj has been on hunger strike since the Saturday before last.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Vincent, can you tell us when you saw Mr. Seselj for the last time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VINCENT
utterances.text: Your Honour, the last time I saw him was at half past four yesterday afternoon, when I visited the Detention Unit and spent something like 40 minutes in his company.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you have a conversation with him at that time?

utterances.speaker: MR. VINCENT
utterances.text: I did have a conversation with him, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I'm not asking about the content of the conversation, but was this a conversation of a type which I would say would normally take place between two persons who understand each other, who express themselves clearly? Of course, I'm especially interested in Mr. Seselj's state of mind. Did he give you the impression that he was able to normally communicate, I would say, at an intellectual level as you would expect normally?

utterances.speaker: MR. VINCENT
utterances.text: He most certainly was, Your Honours. The conversation I'm aware you and your colleagues would not be wanting to inquire into details. The conversation was purely administrative so far as the registry's approach to assisting Mr. Seselj to take part in the trial process. I saw him on Monday and had a conversation slightly shorter with him. Yesterday was a longer conversation. And during that time, and of course there was an interpreter there, during that time we covered a range of subjects and, yes, he certainly gave the impression that he was more than capable of not only partaking in the conversation but understanding the nature of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you tell us -- I know that you're not an expert, so I'm asking you just your impression as a lay person, was Mr. Seselj seated in a chair, was he using any additional tools to -- well, to stand or was he lying down? Could you give us an impression about what a layman would consider to be his physical condition when you spoke to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VINCENT
utterances.text: Certainly, it may help Your Honours if I describe, just very briefly, the conditions under which I saw Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VINCENT
utterances.text: They were very much as when I saw him on the previous day. I was taken to the detention commander's office, a language assistant was provided and I waited for Mr. Seselj to be brought up from his accommodation. He walked up under his own steam, as it were, and came and walked into the detention commander's office and sat down and then conducted the conversation with me. After that, he then got up and left and was then escorted back down to his accommodation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did he use a walking stick or something of that kind?

utterances.speaker: MR. VINCENT
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He didn't. Were you informed by any official of the Detention Unit whether Mr. Seselj used the opportunity to be outdoors, to have fresh an air and were you informed on when he used that opportunity, if at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. VINCENT
utterances.text: The arrangements in place, for Mr. Seselj, Your Honours, is that I receive a report every morning from the Detention Unit as to the whole situation as far as Mr. Seselj and his health and his activities during the previous 24 hours. Certainly, he has not been taking part in any of the sporting sessions on offer but he has been taking advantage of what is known as the fresh air session, so he is -- has been mixing with the other inmates and has been taking that opportunity to get fresh air. I can go into more detail, should you wish, in terms of his activities throughout the 24 hour period, particularly so far as the night-time is concerned, but I await your questions on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then another matter, Mr. Vincent. This Chamber indirectly was informed about a hunger strike, not only this morning by you, but also because administrative decisions have been taken to cope with the situation of the hunger strike. This Chamber has not been informed directly by Mr. Seselj about the reasons for his hunger strike. Did Mr. Seselj inform the Registry about the reasons for his hunger strike?

utterances.speaker: MR. VINCENT
utterances.text: Well, initially, Your Honour, and I'm sure you'll stop me if I'm going back too far, but initially we had a communication from those purporting to represent Mr. Seselj or those who he would want to represent him. And, of course, I don't refer to stand-by counsel in this respect as that was not -- they notified us that, in fact, he was -- he was going on hunger strike. The Registry responded to that, as a matter of courtesy, because it had no legal standing as far as we were concerned. It wasn't a filing. So that was the first official notification that we've had. Since then, through the Detention Unit, and then face to face with Mr. Seselj, he has confirmed, in fact, that he has been on hunger strike.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did he also confirm any reasons given for his hunger strike?

utterances.speaker: MR. VINCENT
utterances.text: Yes. He's made it very clear that his reasons are attached to those requests that he's made on previous occasions appearing before Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you specify a specific request because a lot of requests have been made by Mr. Seselj over time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VINCENT
utterances.text: Well, firstly, Your Honours, was the question of the limitation on the visits by his wife, which was in connection with an order made at the request of the Prosecution. Secondly, he has made a number of requests so far as the translation of documents to enable him to conduct his defence. He has also asked for stand-by counsel to be dismissed. And in addition to that, he has asked for his own legal advisers on his nomination to be authorised to appear before Your Honours. So those -- in summation, those are the four key areas which he has consistently referred to. And, of course, as far as the first matter is concerned, so far as the visitations by his wife are concerned, is that that order has now lapsed and he is well aware because I gave him a letter on Monday of this week that that matter now is something which is now not a matter of concern for him. So it's the three remaining generic requests, accommodation, representation, and the translation of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So the reasons given by Mr. Seselj are matching the reasons given by those who addressed you although without any legal standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VINCENT
utterances.text: Your Honours, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vincent, the information you gave us about the weak state of this morning, how did you receive that information? Did you get that from --

utterances.speaker: MR. VINCENT
utterances.text: That was by telephone, Your Honours, from Mr. McFadden, the detention commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And Mr. McFadden observed what Mr. Seselj said in this respect himself?

utterances.speaker: MR. VINCENT
utterances.text: He did, Your Honours, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vincent, for your answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the present situation, the Chamber would like to issue a warning. The Chamber has been informed that Mr. Seselj is on a hunger strike. The Chamber has also been informed that Mr. Seselj felt too weak to attend the Status Conference. And on the basis of the information this Chamber received and in the absence of any direct message from the accused addressed to the Chamber, the Chamber cannot but conclude that the physical condition of Mr. Seselj is related to his hunger strike. The Chamber considers that whether this self-induced physical condition prevents Mr. Seselj from attending today's hearing, or whether Mr. Seselj has wilfully decided not to attend the hearing, Mr. Seselj's absence, not further explained by him, constitutes disruptive conduct. The Chamber hereby warns Mr. Seselj that his behaviour may result in the temporary takeover of the defence by stand-by counsel during today's Status Conference, in accordance with the Chamber's order of the 25th of October, paragraph 5(h). The Chamber hereby instructs the Registrar to immediately deliver this warning to Mr. Seselj at the United Nations Detention Unit. Should Mr. Seselj wish to appear, he must give immediate notice to the personnel of the United Nations Detention Unit and appear before this Chamber as soon as possible today, before 12.00. The Registrar is then also instructed to arrange for Mr. Seselj to be brought to court. Since it will take some time to deliver this warning to Mr. Seselj, we will adjourn. The parties are requested to stay stand-by and we will not resume any earlier than 10.00. We stand adjourned. --- Break taken at 9.24 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed. The Chamber establishes that Mr. Seselj is not present in the courtroom. Mr. Vincent, could you report back to the Chamber. First question, has the warning that was issued this morning by the Trial Chamber, has it been read out to the accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. VINCENT
utterances.text: Your Honours, yes, it has been read out. It was read firstly by a language assistant in the Detention Unit and it was then followed by a request by Mr. Seselj for that warning to be handed to him in translated form and that was done as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did Mr. Seselj, in any way respond to the warning?

utterances.speaker: MR. VINCENT
utterances.text: He did, Your Honours, and it was in the presence of Klaus Hansen, who is one of the deputy commanders at the Detention Unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you were informed by whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. VINCENT
utterances.text: Mr. Hansen phoned me and gave me the message verbatim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us how Mr. Seselj responded, what language did he use or what was the message?

utterances.speaker: MR. VINCENT
utterances.text: The message was translated, but he spoke to Mr. Hansen and he said -- translation -- and I quote, is, "No, I am not going. They are all idiots if they think that I am going." That's all that he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vincent, first of all, thank you for reporting back to the Chamber. I would like to invite you to stay in this courtroom because there might be some other issues on which we would want to seek further information, which perhaps you could provide to us. But let's first deal with the absence of Mr. Seselj at this moment. The Trial Chamber has now been informed that the warning was read out, the warning that was read out in this courtroom before the break, and has been delivered and read out to the accused in his own language. The Trial Chamber has further been informed by Mr. Vincent that the accused has said that he would not attend today's Status Conference. On the basis of the warning that was issued earlier today, the Trial Chamber hereby decides, in accordance with paragraph 5(h) of the Trial Chamber's order of the 25th of October 2006, that stand-by counsel shall take over the conduct of the defence of the accused for the duration of today's Status Conference. Mr. Hooper, that means that you are activated again and that you're acting counsel at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Understood. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll proceed with the agenda. One of the things the Chamber would like to be informed about, because it was announced earlier that the Registry would present to the accused what facilities he could use when representing himself. Mr. Vincent, could you update the Trial Chamber on whether Mr. Seselj was informed about facilities and what these facilities are, not necessarily to be repeated all in this courtroom, but if, for example, they would be put on paper somewhere, perhaps filing of what was offered to Mr. Seselj might help us out. Could you please report to us?

utterances.speaker: MR. VINCENT
utterances.text: Your Honours, yes. And if you'll bear with me just a second, of course, Mr. Seselj, during the course of a number of appearances, has made a number of requests. And the view taken by the Registry was that perhaps it would help Mr. Seselj, as well as the Trial Chamber and everyone else concerned, if we were able to pull those together into one single response to Mr. Seselj. And so work having been done on that, on the 17th of November, a memorandum was composed which addressed, to the best of the Registry's ability, the matters that Mr. Seselj had raised and that was translated and it was then delivered to -- by me to him on Monday of this week. So that gave him an opportunity to discuss with me, if he required to do so, those particular facilities. Those facilities which, of course, I'm only too prepared to go into in some detail, but basically covered the requests which we discussed before the adjournment that he'd made, which were the question of accommodation in the Detention Unit to enable him to fulfil his self-representation and a number of matters which I'm sure you wouldn't want me to go into too much detail, but obvious things such as telephone, fax, et cetera. And thereafter, of course, the authorisation of those nominated by him to conduct his defence. So it was those kind of facilities that we addressed and I have the memorandum here, the 17th of November, which I'm more than happy to produce to the Court if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vincent, you're invited to file that document so that the Chamber is fully aware of what was offered to Mr. Seselj. And just one additional question. You mentioned a few items. Is equipment which gives access to audio CD-ROMs or video DVD, was that included as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. VINCENT
utterances.text: It's the whole raft of materials, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that. So we would like to see the document. So if you would please be so kind to file it, so that it's among -- it's part of the record of this case. Then I'd like to be updated and briefly informed, although it's not the primary responsibility of this Chamber, although this Chamber of course has and hereby expresses its concerns about the potential damage to the health of Mr. Seselj, which may be caused by his hunger strike. But what the Chamber would like to know is, briefly, what kind of action is taken so as to make sure that no damage will occur which could have been prevented. What action, what measures have been taken in order to look after the condition of Mr. Seselj as good as is possible under the present circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MR. VINCENT
utterances.text: Your Honours, yes, perhaps firstly, and Your Honour referred to make, with respect, quite correctly as a lay person in these matters but I will certainly do my best to -- on the advice of the -- of the doctor at the Unit. Firstly, the term hunger strike has been used fairly extensively outside this Trial Chamber. The line that the Registry is taken on this and always has done is that, in fact, Mr. Seselj has from the outset, refused to take the food that's been offered to him by the Detention Unit. He continues to take fluids, et cetera. It may seem just a, perhaps, a play on words, but certainly that's the approach that we are adopting there, although hunger strike is normally the phrase which is the populist phrase for this. So far as the conditions are concerned, the only difficulty I have, Your Honours, so far as one matter is concerned, which is quite crucial, is a matter which is the subject of a confidential filing by the Registry and with the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If there is -- the Chamber is aware, so it doesn't seek any additional information on any matter which is covered by confidential submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VINCENT
utterances.text: Grateful. Then, Your Honour, the -- there has been a very rigorous routine put in place so far as Mr. Seselj's concerned. The Registry receives a daily report, each morning, on Mr. Seselj's activities, et cetera and ranging from the liquids he's taking to confirmation as to whether he's taking the food on offer or not. In addition to that, I'm also informed as to whether he takes any exercise and indeed in terms of his sleeping habits, et cetera, et cetera. He, of course, continues to refuse any kind of medication of any sort, major or minor, and he has no contact with the medical doctor and nurse, although he does receive them. Dr. Falke, the Detention Unit doctor, has provided us with extensive advice as to how to deal with the situation, because if it does continue, obviously, concerns grow, and indeed, I have only just come from the phone from talking to Dr. Falke about those arrangements and he is more than happy that everything in place meets entirely with the advice from the World Health Organization so far as matters such as this are concerned. We also have and the detention commander has put in place a very rigorous routine so far as all personnel who are responsible for observing Mr. Seselj throughout the 24-hour period of each day, and there has been a very detailed set of operations put in place to deal with any difficulties that may occur in the coming days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for this report, Mr. Vincent. The Chamber has no further questions on the matter. That means that there are no other subjects at this moment on which the Chamber would like to seek information from you. So, please feel free to go, if you want to.

utterances.speaker: MR. VINCENT
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the next issue I'd like to deal with is the preparation of the parties for the commencement of trial, and the Chamber would like to note the following developments. If there is any need to respond to it, the parties are invited to do so. First, the reduced indictment was filed on the 10th of November 2006, in both English and a B/C/S translation. It was provided to the accused on the 13th of November 2006, but not accepted by him until the 14th of November. The accused's application for certification to appeal the Chamber's decision on the request to amend the Prosecution's pre-trial brief was denied on the 14th of November 2006. A decision on payment of expenses will be issued today or within the next few days. The Defence pre-trial brief remains due on the 23rd of November 2006, that is tomorrow. The Chamber will issue a decision setting out its written reasons, or rather, setting out in writing its reasons for its order in relation to the Defence pre-trial brief today. The Pre-Trial Conference will be held on the 27th of November 2006. The Prosecution's opening statement and the accused's unsworn statement remains due on the 27th and the 28th of November 2006 respectively. And the date of testimony of the first Prosecution witness remains the 6th of December 2006. There is an item which I'd like to deal with, but we have to go into private session for a while to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are now in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. All screens are switched off? Yes. On the 13th of October 2006, the Prosecution filed a motion for testimony of Witness VS-053 to be heard via video conference link according to Rule 71 bis. The motion was translated and received by the accused on the 10th of November 2006.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The accused has filed a response to the Prosecution's motion of the 13th of October. The accused's response did not specify the total amount of words but, nevertheless, the Trial Chamber exceptionally accepted the accused's response, since it obviously did not exceed the word limit of 800 words. In his response, the accused opposed the Prosecution's motion and argued that the Prosecution had not shown that the witness was incapable or unprepared to appear before the Tribunal, that the certificate accompanying the motion was unsigned and that the doctor who allegedly had issued the certificate was not identified. The Chamber would like to invite the Prosecution to reply to this response by the accused, specifically in terms of signature, whether the doctor was identified, these matters. Mr. Saxon?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the reference is that the accused appears to make to unsigned and unidentified, merely relates to the fact that the Prosecution redacted the name of the physician who signed the statement, redacted the signature, and redacted the place of that physician's practice. That was so as not to divulge the identity of the witness or the physician or his place of residence to the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was this just -- help me remind. Was this in any way indicated? Did you ask any permission to redact that and was the redaction also meant to be redaction to the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, to the best of my knowledge, there was no specific permission sought to make such a redaction. No, Your Honour. And I believe the -- if I have -- can I have one moment, Your Honour, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The Chamber also received --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution filed this motion and the certificate confidentially, so the certificate was not filed in an unredacted form on an ex parte basis with the Trial Chamber. If the Trial Chamber would like to see an unredacted version of this certificate, we can certainly provide that to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's a bit surprising, Mr. Saxon, that we first have to read the response of the accused and then find out that we were presented with a redacted version of something. We were not aware of it being redacted, and that not one word had been said about this. The Chamber will consider whether it is an appropriate solution, as you suggested, but not after having heard from Mr. Hooper, acting Defence counsel, what his position in this respect would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: I think at present, you, the Judges, should see the unredacted document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And would you be satisfied if it would be filed ex parte so that you couldn't see it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Yes. And the matters we would invite the Chamber to consider is the degree of identification that's potential from the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll consider that, whether we'll follow the suggestion given by Mr. Saxon and commented upon by Mr. Hooper. Then I'd like to move to another request - we are still in private session - to another request for a video conference link.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, actually my colleague, Mr. Saxon, had looked into this matter and we thought, when we filed our motion, that medical documentation may not be necessary for the reasons that I think Mr. Saxon can better discuss because he has looked into the legal issues related to such a motion that we filed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, if you will indulge me briefly for a minute or two. The practice of this Tribunal, although not uniform, and the jurisprudence, generally takes a broad and rather liberal view to requests that a witness be permitted to testify via videolink and please permit me to give you just a few examples in the recent history of this Tribunal. If you go back to April of 2004, in the Strugar case, IT-01-42, the Trial Chamber in that case had arranged to hold a hearing with some expert witnesses to determine if one of the accused was competent to stand trial. At a Status Conference on the 1st of April 2004, pages 4324 to 4325 of the transcript, the Presiding Judge ruled that both the Prosecution and the Defence should call an expert witness to provide expertise at the competency hearing. And the Presiding Judge then said this and I quote, "Expert authors may give evidence by videolink if that is more practical." No higher standard was set, no additional criteria were requested. And, indeed, on the 16th of April in that case, Prosecution made an oral application that its expert witness, Dr. Bennett Bloom be granted permission to testify via videolink from the United States because he was unable to travel to The Hague due to, "A family illness." Strugar Trial Chamber, on that same day, issued a written order finding that it was in the interests of justice, pursuant to Rule 71 bis, to hear the witness via videolink. More recently, Your Honours, in the Milutinovic et al case, on the 25th of October of this year, the Trial Chamber rejected a Prosecution motion seeking permission for a witness to testify via videolink on the grounds that the Prosecution had failed to provide a medical certificate substantiating a witness's claim that he had a heart condition which prevented him from travelling to The Hague. However, Your Honours, that same Trial Chamber, in the same trial, just six days later, on the 1st of November 2006, granted a Prosecution motion for permission for a witness to testify via videolink. And the basis of the Prosecution's motion was that the particular witness had no alternative caretaker for her children, and therefore was unable or unwilling to travel to the Netherlands. No independent evidence of the witness's circumstances were submitted in support of that motion. Even more recently, Your Honours, in the ongoing trial of Milan Martic, the Defence, on the 7th of November, submitted a motion for testimony via videolink for an expert witness, Professor Smilja Avramov. The basis of the motion was simply that the witness's age and ill health prevented her from travelling to The Hague. No independent evidence of the witness's condition was provided. And just 10 days ago, the Trial Chamber granted that motion on the 10th of November, again, finding that it was in the interests of justice that Professor Avramov testify via videolink. So although the jurisprudence and practice is not uniform, Prosecution submits that clearly there is a trend for Trial Chambers to take a rather low threshold when determining when the interests of justice would support the use of videolink testimony. We simply wanted to bring that to Your Honour's attention, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mr. Hooper, would you like to respond to submissions made by Mr. Saxon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Merely that our understanding is that one of criteria for videolink is that the witness is, for example, unable to attend the trial and there has not been a sufficiency of evidence in our submission in respect of this witness to support that. There seems to have been a considerable amount of effort that's gone into not getting him a doctor and thinking of arguments not to get him a doctor, but it's a straightforward, in our submission, probably straightforward act, to get a doctor to him to see if he is in fact capable of coming to give evidence. And on behalf of the accused, we would ask that that, in fact, be the policy adopted in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, since you're on your feet, I take it that you want to reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I hope that my learned colleague was not implying that the Prosecution was in any way trying to dissuade or impede this particular witness's ability or possibility of seeing a doctor. If that was the intention of my learned colleague, certainly I can assure the Chamber that nothing is further from the truth. Second of all, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to have a response to that immediately. Was that your suggestion, Mr. Hooper?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Please proceed, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Second of all, based on the jurisprudence beginning from the Tadic case, this is a disjunctive test, not a conjunctive test. The jurisprudence says a witness that is unable or unwilling to come to The Hague may qualify to testify under videolink. That is my only comment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. The Chamber will consider the matter and decide either to seek more information or to decide on the motion based on the submissions made by the parties until now. I'd like to move now back into public session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to first give a clarification on behalf of the Chamber in relation to a decision on protective measures. I first would like to recall the history of the matter. At the last Status Conference that was on the 8th of November, the Chamber issued additional protective measures for Witness VS-054. Protective measures were first issued in relation to VS-054 in the decision of the Chamber on the 6th of July 2005. The relevant paragraph from the decision reads, "The Prosecution shall disclose to the accused and to the stand-by counsel the identifying information regarding VS-054 no later than 30 days before the commencement of trial or unless otherwise ordered by the Chamber." At the last Status Conference, the Chamber was called upon to consider a deadline for the Defence to submit a pre-trial brief. In setting the deadline for the brief, the issue of a start date for the trial was also considered and was set for the 27th of November. Hence, a firm start date for the commencement of trial, subsequent to the Appeals Chamber decision of the 20th of October, was only confirmed on the 8th of November. At this point, the date for disclosure, 30 days prior to the commencement of trial, became due, and the Chamber therefore ordered the immediate disclosure of material relating to Witness VS-054 to the accused. The Chamber is aware that disclosure of material in relation to VS-054, which was completed on the 8th of November, is less than 30 days before the commencement of trial. Commencement of trial set for the 27th of November. In scheduling the start of the date of trial, the Chamber weighed the possibility of a further delay to the commencement of the trial against a previous order to disclose material to the accused on a protected witness not later than 30 days before trial. In reaching its decision, the Chamber considered the necessity of avoiding any further delays to the start of trial as more important than allowing the full 30 days to review disclosed material. Moreover, the Chamber considered the issue of whether a start date of the 27th of November allowed adequate time for the accused to prepare for Witness VS-054. In this regard, the fact that the first witness is not scheduled to appear until the 6th of December also influenced the Chamber's decision, as did the fact that the trial is beginning in a staggered manner, sitting only two days a week in the first week of the trial and three days in the second week. For these reasons, the Chamber considers that the need for a timely commencement of trial and consideration of the fact that the accused would have a sufficient period of time to prepare for the witness before the witness is heard, justifies the disclosure in relation to VS-054 less than 30 days prior to the commencement of trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber adds that, if necessary, the Chamber will revisit the issue of whether the Defence has had adequate time to prepare for the cross-examination of this witness once that witness has appeared to testify. Yes, Mr. Saxon?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the interests of transparency, I must inform the Chamber of one matter. That is simply that today the Prosecution will attempt to provide some hard copy disclosure to the accused Seselj, and in that disclosure, there are several documents that also pertain to VS-054. It is not a lot of material, but it is material that the accused would be getting for the first time and I must inform the Chamber of that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was not included in the 8th of November disclosure?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour. It was mentioned on our exhibit list, but it was not disclosed on the 8th of November, and it is something that we have realised by reviewing our disclosure work over the past few days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that was just by mistake?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour. And it is also by mistake and also because exhibits have come to the attention of the Prosecution during witness proofing more recently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Mr. Hooper?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Yes. Can I also draw to your attention that there was another oversight and that was that none of the material relating to VS-54 was served on stand-by counsel, on us. And we drew the attention of the Prosecution to this, as a result of which, I think we received a CD of disclosure on the 17th of November, on Friday, and we further discussed the position this morning. I've indicated that, as best as we are able, that is as stand-by counsel, and you'll appreciate the implication of that, that we would try and accommodate the Prosecution, but that from our standpoint, we might invite the Chamber to hold the Prosecution to their duty to give us better notice than the 17th of November for this witness and that we couldn't guarantee that the accused would necessarily go along in any event with any accommodation that we might propose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You reserve your position, Mr. Hooper?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear. Mr. Saxon, was that by mistake as well, assuming that what Mr. Hooper just told us reflects what happened?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, simply an oversight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Saxon, there is a theatre play which is called, "A comedy of errors." The OTP should take care that this trial will not become a tragedy of errors. The Chamber would like to be informed specifically on what material was disclosed only later to the accused, to have full information on what he missed in first instance and what he received only later. Yes? Not necessarily now. You can put it down on paper and that the Chamber at least is informed about it. Yes? Any other matter on this 30-day disclosure issue? If not, I'd like to move to another item, which may appear not to be very relevant in the absence of the accused, but the Chamber would like to have the accused provided with a video recording of this Status Conference so that he's fully informed on whatever happened here and for that reason, I'll go into that matter anyhow. On the 10th of November of this year, the Registry returned four submissions to the accused that had been submitted on the 6th of November 2006. The submissions numbering 209 to 212 were returned because they exceeded the word limit or because they did not state the word count in compliance with the Chamber's decision of the 19th of June of this year. That decision set a word limit of 800 words for filings by the accused, unless prior authorisation had been granted to exceed the word limit on the basis of good cause, and that each filing contains a word count at the end of the submission before the signature line. Three of the accused's submissions ranged from 30.000 to 72.000 words. Two of these submissions were responses to the reports of Prosecution expert witnesses Anthony Oberschall and Ives Tomic and one was a response to the Prosecution's motion on adjudicated facts. In relation to the expert reports, Mr. Seselj, in the past, at a Status Conference on the 4th of July of this year, indicated that he intended to cross-examine these two expert witnesses, found on transcript page 546. Also, on the 24th of March 2006, Mr. Seselj filed a submission on the expert report of Mr. Oberschall, indicating that he objected to the report and intended to cross-examine the expert witness. The Trial Chamber hereby decides that the two expert witnesses I just mentioned shall be called for cross-examination. Another one of the filings made by the accused on the 6th of November 2006, I'm referring to submission number 201 -- 210, was a response to the Prosecution's motion on adjudicated facts. On the 12th of July of this year, the Trial Chamber had issued a decision granting the accused a specific exception to file a response to the Prosecution's motion on adjudicated facts of up to 5.000 words. The filing that was returned to the accused was 47.193 words. At the Status Conference on the 4th of July, the accused was instructed how to proceed when responding to a motion on adjudicated facts. I informed Mr. Seselj that he should focus on the criteria which are accepted in the case law of the Tribunal for the admission of adjudicated facts and mentioned, for example, that it should be facts rather than legal findings and that it should not be facts established on the basis of a plea agreement. I also informed the accused that facts established in first instance cannot be taken judicial notice of unless the Appeals Chamber has confirmed them or if they are not challenged on appeal. Furthermore, I informed Mr. Seselj on the 4th of July, that even if an adjudicated fact has been taken judicial notice of, that there still is an opportunity, although within certain limits, to challenge that fact during trial. The filing of Mr. Seselj on the 6th of November was more than 47.000 words instead of the exceptional 5.000 words limit that was set by the Chamber. The other two filings on expert witnesses were also tens of thousands of words over the usual 800-word limit. In this respect, the Chamber also recalls the response by the accused to the Prosecution's motion for the testimony of Witness VS-053 to be heard via video conference. That submission was without a word count and also in violation of the Chamber's decision on the 19th of June 2006. The Chamber anyway accepted that response for reasons given before, and the Chamber does not consider the violation in itself serious enough for a warning. However, here, the Chamber considers the violation, together with other violations of the decision of the 19th of June 2006. The Chamber therefore warns the accused, which will be able to hear this warning by watching the video that will be provided to him, warns the accused, that a persistent non-compliance with the Chamber's decision on word limits is a form of obstructionist conduct. In our decision on assignment of counsel, a decision that has been reversed, the Chamber identified the ongoing filing of oversized motions as persistently abusive. If the accused would continue to submit oversized filings, the Chamber may consider imposing counsel upon the accused, of course, after having given an opportunity for him to be heard. I move to the next item.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To the extent that there may have been any confusion when I just referred to the decision to assign counsel, where I said that the decision was reversed, that the Appeals Chamber did not reverse the decision on incorrectness of the findings of the Chamber in this respect. That's the reason why the Chamber, at this moment, refers to that decision, although for other reasons, the decision finally due to the decision of the Appeals Chamber became ineffective. The Chamber has considered to provide an opportunity to the accused, although the situation of course at this moment is a bit unclear, we have considered the possibility to allow the accused to again submit a response to the Prosecution motion for adjudicated facts, but then to stay within the 5.000 word limit. In the absence of the accused, we'll not finally decide this matter. But the Chamber seriously has considered it, and the accused is informed about it by this. The next issue is about the application for a certification to appeal the Chamber's decision on the form of disclosure. At the 4th of July Status Conference, Mr. Seselj expressed his intention to apply for certification to appeal the Chamber's decision on the form of disclosure of the same date. No reasoned request was received, so the Chamber issued no decision. In a submission dated the 31st of July 2006, the accused purported to appeal the Chamber's decision on the form of disclosure directly to the Appeals Chamber. The submission was returned to the accused because no certificate had been granted. In view of the importance of the decision on the form of disclosure, the Chamber has reconsidered the request by the accused. The Chamber notes that no reasons have been given by the accused for granting his request for certification. But the Chamber anyway decides to grant such a certification as the decision concerns the adequate time and facilities for the preparation of the Defence and an immediate resolution by the Appeals Chamber would prevent that the Trial Chamber proceeds on a wrong procedural basis. The Chamber has considered that the rule allows to grant a certificate and does not prevent from granting a certificate even if an accused has not given proper reasons for a certificate. The next item on the agenda would be the status of responses to motions and new time limits for the accused. Since at this moment the accused is not self-represented, I will not deal with most of the pending issues in this respect, but I'd like to pay attention to two motions that have to be declared moot. There are two motions which were filed in early October during the period where the accused was represented by assigned counsel which remain pending. First, assigned counsel filed a motion on the 10th of October 2006 requesting a medical report on Dr. Seselj. The Prosecution responded on the 13th of October 2006. Secondly, a motion was filed by the Prosecution on the 6th of October 2006, concerning possible threats and intimidation of witnesses and an order for non-disclosure. The motion requests the Chamber to order assigned counsel not to disclose to the accused the order of forthcoming witnesses, and assigned counsel responded on the 9th of October. The Prosecution replied on the 12th of October. In light of the Appeals Chamber decision of the 20th of October 2006, reversing the Trial Chamber's decision on assignment of counsel, and keeping in mind that the activation of stand-by counsel at this moment lasts for this Status Conference only for the time being, these two motions can provisionally be declared moot, depending on what will happen in the near future, as assigned counsel is no longer representing the accused and the accused, although suspended temporarily, is representing himself. The Chamber will further consider this matter, whether it needs any further follow-up. I am now moving to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will move to our next subject, which is the disclosure of the witness order. The Trial Chamber requests the Prosecution to file a list of the names or codes of the witnesses, included on the list of the 9th of May 2006, that they no longer intend to call due to the reduction of the indictment or for any other reason. The Trial Chamber, the accused and stand-by counsel have been informed about the names and the order of the nine witnesses who will testify in December through a letter of the Prosecution to the registrar dated the 17th of November 2006. The Trial Chamber is hereby requesting the Prosecution to provide the Trial Chamber, the accused, and stand-by counsel with such regular updates. These updates should be dated and contain the following information: 1, the name of the witness; 2, the pseudonym of the witness; 3, any protective measures granted; 4, the expected date of testimony; 5, the expected time needed for the examination-in-chief. The update should be provided no later than two weeks before the commencement of the testimony. If the Prosecution intends to change the witness order within this two week period, it should ask for the Trial Chamber's permission to do so. I move to the next item, and I'm wondering whether we have to go into private session. Perhaps out of an abundance of caution, we would go into private session, and if it would not be needed, we'll later decide that this part of the record will become public again. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are now in private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. The item is about the Prosecution's notice regarding protective measures for Witness VS-017 with an ex parte annex. On the 16th of December 2004, the Trial Chamber granted the use of a pseudonym for Witness 17 as well as the late disclosure of the witness information until 30 days before the start of the trial. On the 8th of November of this year, the Trial Chamber also granted the use of face and voice distortion for the witness. On the 14th of November 2006, however, the Prosecution filed a notice regarding these protective measures, informing the Trial Chamber that Witness 17 has since indicated that he wants to testify in public without any protective measures, but he requested that all protective measures ordered by the Trial Chamber remain in effect until the commencement of his testimony. The Chamber would like to receive a response to this request from the Defence. Mr. Hooper?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Well, it seems that these are matters to be decided when the witness is here and before the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, there are two items. The first is that the witness has indicated that he doesn't need any protective measures anymore. At the same time, the Prosecution asks the protective measures to remain in place until the beginning of the testimony. One could think that if there is no -- it's at least --

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I misunderstood. I thought they were both coming from the witness, that they were contradictory, but coming from the same witness. I hadn't appreciated it was the Prosecution who was asking that matters stay in place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, as a matter of fact, that's what the witness invited the Prosecution to ask the Chamber to do. That is to now already decide that the testimony would be given in public, so therefore, that the reasons for protective measures do not exist any longer, but only on from the moment that he appears to testify, which is at least a new situation asking for different -- for different reasons, protective measures only to be in place temporarily and not during the testimony. And the Chamber just wanted to know what position the Defence takes in this respect. And if you would like to take more time to think about it and then inform the Chamber, then no decision has yet been taken. All protective measures are still in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Yes. The status quo can remain. I have no objection to that, bearing in mind what the witness has said he'll do once he's here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: I won't stand in the way of that at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you do not oppose the --

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- request by the Prosecution that protective measures should be lifted but only on from the moment that the testimony of the witness begins?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the Trial Chamber hereby orders that the protective measures ordered on the 16th of December 2004, and the 8th of November 2006, shall remain in place until the moment Witness 17 will commence his testimony, at which moment, they will be lifted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will need a break anyhow. We are still in private session. We can return to open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will need a break anyhow. Therefore, we will adjourn until ten minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Unfortunately, the Chamber could not be ready earlier than 15 minutes after the time announced to resume. I'd now like to move to the next subject, that's the issue of special defences. The Chamber renders hereby its decision on the question whether the accused has notified the Prosecution of an alibi defence or any special defence, in accordance with Rule 67(A)(i) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Rule 67 of the Rules creates an obligation for the Defence to notify the Prosecution of an intention to offer a defence of alibi or any special defence and to disclose additional information relating to such defences. In turn, the Prosecution is under the obligation, if it intends to rebut the alibi defence or the special defence invoked, to notify the Defence of its rebuttal evidence. According to the Prosecution, since September 2003, the accused has served on it 15 submissions containing over 5.500 pages and which, according to the accused, constitute notifications of a special defence under the aforementioned Rule. At the Status Conferences held on the 3rd and the 8th of November 2006, the parties submitted their views in relation to those submissions. On the 7th of November 2006, the Prosecution filed an additional submission further clarifying its position on this matter. The accused informed us that the material he submitted contains references to various documents and books that will be used mostly in the cross-examination of the Prosecution expert witnesses. The accused's submissions do not contain any references to witnesses that could testify in support of the material. The accused submits further that his special defence includes the following topics: 1, historical context and circumstances; 2, analysis of alleged hate speeches in the western press and by western Muslim and Croat politicians; 3, joint criminal enterprise and; 4, the accused's public speeches about the war and the obligations to abide by the laws of war. According to the accused, his defence is special as it is a defence which has never been presented at the Tribunal before. The Prosecution does not consider the accused's submissions to be a special defence within the meaning of Rule 67 of the Rules. According to the Prosecution, they consist of hundreds of pages of quotations from the accused's books, copies of prior speeches, et cetera. Also, according to the Prosecution, the material contains repeated allegations against the Pope and the Roman Catholic church. The Prosecution argues further that the accused's submissions, and I quote, "address issues raised in the indictment and in the Prosecution's pre-trial brief," and are more analogous to a defence pre-trial brief than any kind of notice pertaining to a special defence. At the Status Conferences on the 3rd and the 8th of November 2006 the Chamber gave the accused ample opportunities to identify and clarify what, according to him, is his special defence. The accused appears to be confusing the concept of a special defence with that of a unique defence. A defence cannot be considered to be a special defence within the meaning of Rule 67 of the Rules merely because it is a defence that is being argued for the first time before the Tribunal. The Chamber has reviewed the translated submissions of the accused. Submissions 103 and 104 challenge the credibility of potential Prosecution witnesses. Submissions 147 deals with the, and I quote, "Role of the Vatican and Pope John-Paul II in the crimes committed in the territory of the former Yugoslavia in 1991." None of the four topics mentioned earlier, which represent the accused's oral submissions, constitute special defences. Rather, as the Prosecution has submitted, they are more analogous to submissions made in a defence pre-trial brief. Therefore, no prior notice to the Prosecution was necessary. The Chamber concludes that the accused has failed to identify any special defence. And this concludes the Chamber's decision on this matter. Next item I'd like to deal with is the translation of jurisprudence. During the last Status Conference on the 8th of November 2006, the accused asked for the Trial Chamber judgement in the Limaj case. The Trial Chamber reminds the accused that the matter of him being provided with translations of the case law of the Tribunal has been decided on in decisions on the 9th of November 2005 and the 12th of July 2006. The matter has also been addressed by the Registrar. These were the items I had on my mind to deal with, but I'd like to invite the parties to raise any other issue. Yes, there is one issue that I'd forgotten to raise. When I earlier instructed the Prosecution to give updates on the witness lists, which witness to come to testify when, I'd like to add that the Prosecution is also required to indicate what documents it intends to present through that witness, in those witness updates, so that the Chamber is always fully aware of what to expect. Is that clear? It's in addition to what I said before.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That's clear, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Then, for the parties, Mr. Saxon or Madam Uertz-Retzlaff, is there anything you would like to raise at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hooper?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Yes, there is one matter, Your Honour, and that relates to the special defences that you've referred to already just a moment ago. And also to the overlong motions or responses to motions by the accused that were received by the Registry but were returned to him. In respect of the first matters, a number of those, I understand, have been translated. I don't have the precise details to mind at the moment, but I know -- I believe on our last Status Conference, there was reference made to that, but there were some that were not. And I'd ask that those matters be provided in a translated form, i.e., in English, to stand-by counsel. In respect of the overlong motions or responses, those were returned, as I understand it, to the accused, and if that word is used appropriately, then the Registry will not be in possession of them, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that the procedure is that if submissions are not filed and returned to a party, that a copy is kept for administrative purposes by the Registry, because if there would ever be any dispute about whether it was correct or not correct to send something back, that at least, the Registrar should know what we are talking about. So unless Mr. Registrar or the representative of the Registry would contradict me now, that's what I understand procedure to be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour is absolutely correct. We do --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please remove the headphones away.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Documents have been returned to Mr. Seselj and we will have it provided to stand-by counsel at the end of the hearing today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps, I interfere for one more moment. If a lengthy submission is sent back, then it doesn't mean that it has been translated into English. Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Hooper.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: No, but somewhere we hope, that in the archives, there will be a photocopy or copy of the original document, presumably in Serbian, and we would ask that that be made available to stand-by counsel and translated for stand-by counsel into English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, one of the reasons why there are limits on -- I'm not saying all the reasons, but one of the reasons certainly is that it would exhaust the resources of this Tribunal if 5.000 pages or 7.000 pages first have to be translated and only then for us to find out that they may be irrelevant or that would -- that would drain the resources of the Tribunal. So, therefore, of course, I understand that you'd like to know what's in these submissions, whether that should be achieved by having them in full translated is not self-explanatory.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Well the reason is, of course, as stand-by counsel, that may have a limited effect, but looking at the trial as a whole, and the possible avenues that it may take, then overall, we would submit, that it's in the interests of the accused that those matters be translated and provided to stand-by counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Another option would be that the accused informs, in summary form, stand-by counsel, if he considers that it would be of any use for his defence that stand-by counsel is aware of the content of these materials. But it's -- this Chamber is not the master over the CLSS, which is responsible for preparing translations, and there are policies in which I would like not to dive in at this moment, but it's on the record that you take the position that it would serve the way you perform your task in being provided with a translation of those submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Yes. And I appreciate there are difficulties here, particularly with the translation service and the demands made upon it. And perhaps, therefore, I can restrict my application this morning to service of those documents, those categories of documents, special defences and the rejected documents relating to the accused, that they be provided to stand-by counsel. We do have someone who can read sufficient or can read Serbian and will be in a position, on reflection at least, to identify perhaps further and better those matters that perhaps in due course become particularly pertinent and relevant and necessary to translate. So I withdraw the application to have the matters translated at this stage and merely seek to preserve the serving of the documents as a matter of course on stand-by counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From what I understand, some of the submissions were filed and therefore these are translated, and the Chamber could read them, but some of these are just sent to the Prosecution, have not been filed, so I take it that the registrar will consider to provide you the copies of the originals that were sent back. Of course, the ones that have been filed and are referred to by the accused as containing special defences, of course, are already available, to the extent that they are only sent to the Prosecution, I think it would be Mr. Saxon or Madam Uertz-Retzlaff who would have the response.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, in regard to 15 submissions that were provided to the Prosecution, if it would facilitate matters, we can provide these to stand-by counsel on a CD-ROM or a DVD. So that might make their life easier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So they will be provided but in electronic format. Any other issue, Mr. Hooper, you would like to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, there being nothing else on the agenda, the Chamber would like to inform Prosecution and Defence that the accused will be invited to make submissions in writing or orally under paragraph 5(i) of the Chamber's order of the 25th of October 2006. An invitation, a written invitation to this effect will be issued later today, and it contains an invitation to make submissions by next Friday in writing and/or to add anything orally -- when I said next Friday, I meant this Friday -- so to make submissions by this Friday in writing or, if the accused would prefer to add oral submissions, to do that at the Pre-Trial Conference or, if he doesn't make any written submissions to make oral submissions Monday at the Pre-Trial Conference. We stand adjourned until next Monday at the Pre-Trial Conference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: adjourned at 1.23 p.m. 25

procedural_notes.text: [Private session] [Confidentiality partially lifted by order of Trial Chamber]
[Private session] [Confidentiality lifted by order of Trial Chamber]
